description: Tracing JIT decomposed. Trace recording, trace compilation, guards, deoptimisation, side exits, trace stitching. LuaJIT's design as the canonical example. Why tracing JITs excel at hot inner loops in dynamic languages + fail when traces don't form.

sub_mechanisms.name: trace_recording
sub_mechanisms.definition: When a hot loop is detected, record the exact sequence of instructions executed during the next iteration. Each operation is captured.
sub_mechanisms.why: Specialises to the actually-executed path. Cuts across function boundaries (inlining). Captures observed types. The recording mode is the JIT's information-gathering phase.

sub_mechanisms.name: trace_anchor
sub_mechanisms.definition: Point where tracing begins (typically a loop back-edge). Subsequent execution is recorded into the trace until reaching the anchor again.
sub_mechanisms.why: Loop-centric: traces represent loop iterations. Anchor + body form the optimisation unit. Function entry can also be an anchor for non-loop hot paths.

sub_mechanisms.name: guard
sub_mechanisms.definition: Runtime check inserted into the trace that the assumption (type, value, control flow) holds. On failure, exit the trace.
sub_mechanisms.why: Trace specialises to observed conditions. Guard verifies they still hold. Compiles to a single compare + jump in fast path; failure jumps to deoptimisation. Critical for trace correctness.

sub_mechanisms.name: side_exit
sub_mechanisms.definition: When a guard fails, the trace exits to the interpreter or a different trace. Side exits are jump targets.
sub_mechanisms.why: Failed assumption means optimised code can't continue. Side exit transfers control safely. Implementation: each guard generates a small exit stub that restores interpreter state.

sub_mechanisms.name: trace_compilation
sub_mechanisms.definition: After recording, optimise + compile the trace. Linear code (no branches except guards) — easier than general optimisation.
sub_mechanisms.why: Linear traces are easier to optimise than general CFGs. Constant propagation, CSE, scalar replacement all straightforward. The simplicity is part of tracing JIT's appeal.

sub_mechanisms.name: trace_specialisation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Trace assumes specific types + values observed during recording. e.g., recorded with x being an integer, trace assumes integer for all subsequent execution.
sub_mechanisms.why: Specialised code is fast (no dispatch, direct ops). Guards enforce the assumption. Win when assumption holds; cost when it doesn't (deopt + retrace).

sub_mechanisms.name: trace_stitching
sub_mechanisms.definition: Chain multiple traces together: end of trace A jumps to start of trace B if the appropriate condition holds.
sub_mechanisms.why: Complex control flow has multiple traces (one per common path). Stitching connects them, eliminating interpreter round-trips between traces. PyPy + LuaJIT use this extensively.

sub_mechanisms.name: trace_explosion
sub_mechanisms.definition: Pathological case: highly variable execution patterns generate many traces, each covering small fraction of execution. Compile cost dominates.
sub_mechanisms.why: Tracing assumes most execution follows few hot paths. When this fails (highly polymorphic code), the JIT produces too many specialised traces. Threshold tuning + giving up to fall back to interpreter mitigate.

sub_mechanisms.name: LuaJIT_design
sub_mechanisms.definition: Mike Pall's tracing JIT for Lua. Records bytecode-level traces, compiles via a sophisticated IR (LuaJIT IR), emits machine code directly.
sub_mechanisms.why: Often the fastest JIT for dynamic-language code. Demonstrates tracing's strengths. LuaJIT outperforms many statically-compiled languages on suitable workloads. Influenced PyPy + many later JITs.

sub_mechanisms.name: PyPy_meta_tracing
sub_mechanisms.definition: PyPy's approach: generate a tracing JIT from an interpreter description. The JIT traces the interpreter's execution of user code.
sub_mechanisms.why: Meta-tracing means writing one tracing JIT generator + many interpreters get tracing for free. PyPy applies this to Python; the resulting JIT exceeds CPython by 10x+ on hot code. Generalises tracing to any interpreter.

sub_mechanisms.name: TraceMonkey_history
sub_mechanisms.definition: Early Firefox JavaScript JIT (2008). Pioneered tracing for JavaScript. Replaced by IonMonkey (method JIT) in 2012.
sub_mechanisms.why: Historical: traced JavaScript was viable but had trace-explosion issues on real web code. Method JIT (whole-function compilation) proved more robust for the JS ecosystem. Tracing remained dominant for Lua.

sub_mechanisms.name: blackhole_interpreter
sub_mechanisms.definition: Interpreter state at the side-exit point, used to resume execution when a trace deoptimises.
sub_mechanisms.why: Deoptimisation requires reconstructing the interpreter's view. Blackhole interp runs from the side-exit's state. Critical for correctness: optimised code must safely transition back to interpreter on assumption failure.

derivation_rules.name: tracing_specialises_to_observed_path
if: a trace records execution through one specific control-flow path
then: compiled code is specialised to that path
derivation_rules.why: Linear trace has no branches except guards. Aggressive optimisations (constant propagation, scalar replacement, inlining) apply without merge-point complications. Optimised trace beats general compilation for the recorded path.

derivation_rules.name: guards_enable_specialisation_safely
then: trace specialisation based on that assumption is sound
derivation_rules.why: Without guards, specialised code could execute on wrong types/values. Guards check at runtime; failure exits to safe code. Trade-off: more guards = more overhead; fewer = less safe. JITs tune guard placement carefully.

derivation_rules.name: tracing_excels_on_loop_intensive_dynamic_code
if: program has hot inner loops with consistent types
derivation_rules.why: Traces capture exactly the hot path; guards specialise to observed types. LuaJIT outperforms most JITs on numeric Lua code for this reason. Loop-heavy benchmarks favour tracing; control-flow-heavy code favours method JITs.

derivation_rules.name: trace_explosion_limits_tracing_applicability
if: program has highly variable execution paths
then: tracing JIT produces many specialised traces; performance degrades
derivation_rules.why: Each unique path becomes a trace. Compile cost grows; cache locality drops; fallback to interpreter common. Method JITs handle this better — they compile whole functions, not paths. TraceMonkey's failure on real web code drove Firefox to method JITs.

derivation_rules.name: meta_tracing_amortises_JIT_construction
if: a meta-tracing system traces an interpreter's execution
then: the interpreter implicitly defines a JIT for its language
derivation_rules.why: Write the interpreter once, get JIT for free via meta-tracing. PyPy demonstrates this for Python. RPython framework generates the tracing JIT from interpreter source. Generalises tracing to any interpreter without rewriting the JIT for each language.
